data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":{"adopted_commitment_refs":[],"disanalogies":["Biological evolution has no conscious goal of error elimination, whereas Popperian science does.","Natural selection operates on reproduction rates, while scientific selection operates on logical consistency and test severity.","Evolutionary fitness is relative to a specific environment, while scientific corroboration aims for universal scope."],"overturn_conditions":["If biological survival actually implies a probabilistic increase in future survival capabilities beyond the immediate context.","If the analogy requires a teleological element that Popper explicitly forbids in methodology."],"shared_structure":["Selection based on survival of stress rather than prediction of future survival.","Distinction between descriptive history and normative rule.","Rejection of probabilistic weighting in favor of binary status (falsified/not-yet-falsified)."],"source_memory_refs":["SRC_014","SRC_009"],"transfer_claims":["Just as a species surviving a plague isn't 'probabilistically guaranteed' to survive the next, a corroborated theory isn't probable, but it is the best candidate to reveal new flaws.","The 'preference' in evolution is descriptive; in Popper, it is a prescriptive rule adopted by the critic."]},"claim":"Popper's preference for better-corroborated theories is defensible on his own terms not as an inductive inference of future success, but as a non-inductive methodological rule to maximize the severity of future tests; accepting this costs us the assurance that science converges toward truth or practical reliability, leaving us with only a procedural commitment to error-elimination without epistemic probability.","counterconditions":[{"case":"If the preference implies any increase in the logical probability of the theory being true.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the choice relies on an implicit assumption that past test results correlate with future performance (uniformity of nature).","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the 'methodological rule' cannot be distinguished from Poincar\u00e9an conventionalism where rules are arbitrary rather than truth-seeking.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the account fails to explain why Popper himself acted as if corroborated theories were more reliable.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"The mechanism distinguishes between 'rational belief' (which Popper rejects as inductive) and 'rational action' (which he accepts as critical). By framing the preference as a decision to subject the most vulnerable (best-tested) theory to new attempts at falsification, the scientist avoids assuming nature is uniform. Instead, they adopt a convention: 'If we must choose a basis for action, choose the one that has survived the hardest attempts to kill it, because if it is false, we are most likely to find out soon.' This transforms the preference from a prediction of success into a strategy for rapid error detection.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
